# Pancreatic Cancer: Epidemiology

## Overview: The Pancreas
- Located in the retroperitoneum
- Has both exocrine and endocrine functions
- Exocrine pancreas:
  - Composed of duct cells and acinar cells
  - Produce enzymes to break down carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids
  - Promotes digestion
- Majority of malignant pancreatic neoplasms arise from the exocrine component

## Overview: Types of Pancreatic Neoplasms
- Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC):
  - Most common type of pancreatic cancer (PC)
  - Represents >90% of exocrine pancreas cases
- Other exocrine tumors (10%):
  - Mucinous tumors
  - Mixed adenosquamous tumors
  - Acinar cell tumors
- Endocrine neoplasms:
  - Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors
  - Contribute ~5% of total PC cases

## US Cancer Statistics (2017-2020)
- 2,820,034 deaths in US (2017): 21% from cancer
- Cancer death rate declined 29% from 1991 to 2017
- PDAC accounts for:
  - 3.0% of all new cancers
  - 8% of all cancer deaths in the US
- 4th leading cause of cancer death in men and women (as of 2014)
- 2020 Predictions: >57,600 new cases, ~47,050 deaths

## PDAC Mortality and Survival Trends
- Diagnosis confers an unfavorable prognosis
- Death rate increased 0.4% between 1998 and 2017
- 5-year survival rate has tripled to 9.3% in the past 10 years
- Predicted to become the 2nd leading cause of cancer death by 2030
- Reasons for poor progress:
  - Improved survival in other leading cancers
  - Limited success in chemo/radiotherapy for PDAC
  - Multilayered therapeutic resistance

## Therapeutic Resistance Challenges
- PDAC is characterized by multilayered therapeutic resistance
- Factors contributing to resistance include:
  - Dense, desmoplastic tumor stroma
  - Hypoxic environment
  - Reduced vascular density
  - Immune suppression
  - Early, undetected microscopic metastases
- Current research targeting these challenges offers hope for progress

## Global Incidence and Mortality (2018)
- 7th leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide
- 432,242 deaths in 2018 (2.5% of all cancers)
- 458,918 new cases reported in 2018
- Annual incidence rate: ~4.9 new cases per 100,000 persons
- Ranks 12th among all cancers globally
- More common in men (5.5) than women (4.0) per 100,000

## Nonmodifiable Risk Factors: Gender
- US National Center for Health Statistics (2020 estimates):
  - Men: 30,400 new cases
  - Women: 27,200 new cases
  - Accounts for 3% of all cancers in the US
- US Population Risk:
  - Men: 14.0 per 100,000
  - Women: 10.7 per 100,000
- High development index countries:
  - Women have 5x greater risk than women in lower development index countries
- Reproductive factors:
  - Systematic review found NO reproductive factors associated with PC risk in women

## Nonmodifiable Risk Factors: Age
- Main risk factor for PC is advancing age
- Peak incidence in US: 7th and 8th decades of life
- Median age at diagnosis: 71 years (2007-2011 SEER data)
- Median age at death: 73 years
- >60% of new PDAC cases occur between ages 65 and 84 years
- Peak age varies by country (e.g., India: 6th decade)
- Emerging age-specific trends in US:
  - Individuals 20 to 29 years old
  - Persons over the age of 80 years

## Race and Ethnicity: Incidence
- Highest incidence: Black Americans
  - Men: 17.2 per 100,000
  - Women: 14.2 per 100,000
- Lowest risk: Asian/Pacific Islander
  - Men: 10.7 per 100,000
  - Women: 8.9 per 100,000
- Death rates (per 100,000):
  - African American men: 15.5
  - African American women: 12.6
  - White men: 12.4
  - White women: 9.3

## Race and Ethnicity: African Americans
- Highest death rates from cancer overall
- Shortest survival period of all racial groups
- Higher incidence rates for all cancers combined
- Higher incidence for most common cancers (prostate, lung, colorectal, pancreas)
- Lower socioeconomic status correlates with:
  - Advanced stage diagnosis
  - Less likely to undergo surgery
  - Less likely to receive chemotherapy
- Higher prevalence of other risk factors: obesity, diabetes, pancreatitis

## Race and Ethnicity: Smoking Metabolism
- Serum cotinine levels (nicotine metabolite):
  - Consistently higher in African Americans than Whites and Mexican Americans
  - Remains higher even after adjusting for:
    - Cigarettes smoked per day
    - Smokers in the home
    - ETS exposure at work
    - Rooms in home, region of country
- Suggests genetic differences in cigarette product metabolism may influence PDAC rates

## Race and Ethnicity: Ashkenazi Jews
- PC occurs more commonly in Jewish population, especially Ashkenazi heritage
- Age-standardized rates in Israel:
  - Jewish men: 7.2 | Jewish women: 5.7
  - Non-Jewish men: 4.0 | Non-Jewish women: 2.9
- 5% to 10% of discrepancy attributed to BRCA2 mutation (6174delT)
- 6174delT is present in ~1% of Ashkenazi Jews and ~4% of all PDAC patients
- Associated with breast, gastric, ovarian, and bile duct cancers
- BRCA1 founder mutations occur less commonly (1.3% in Jewish PC patients)

## Race and Ethnicity: Asians
- Asian patients reported to have:
  - Less aggressive tumors than non-Asians
  - Higher survival rates on a stage-adjusted basis
- SEER population-based study (Hawaii, SF, Seattle):
  - Japanese patients: highest fraction of localized tumors, lowest grade
  - Chinese, Filipino, Japanese women: longer survival times than Whites
- Reasons unknown, but race-related genetic and environmental exposure factors are suspected causes

## Risk Factors: Etiology and Pathways
- Etiology is multifactorial
- Common underlying pathways:
  - Insulin resistance
  - Inflammation
  - Hemostasis
  - Infection
- Characterized by multiple germline and somatic genetic mutations
- Sporadic vs. Hereditary:
  - >80% due to sporadically occurring mutations
  - <3% truly hereditary (inherited germline mutations/syndromes)

## Risk Factors: Germline Mutations
- 2015 investigation of germline mutations in PC patients:
  - 11 pathogenic mutations found (ATM, BRCA1, BRCA2, MLH1, MSH6, TP53)
  - Mutation carrier rate: 3.8%
- None correlated with known family history, age at diagnosis, or stage
- No carriers of PALB2, CDK2NA, PRSS1, or STK11 in this specific cohort
- Personal risk factors include: tobacco, ETS, occupational carcinogens, race, diet, obesity, alcohol, pancreatitis, diabetes, blood group, infections

- Cigarette smoking (dose-response relationship)
- Environmental tobacco smoke (ETS), particularly early in life

- Height (RR 1.81 comparing tallest vs shortest categories)
- Previous Surgery: Cholecystectomy, Gastrectomy

## Familial Pancreatic Cancer: Definitions
- Generally considered familial if:
  - ≥2 first-degree relatives (mother, father, sister, brother) have confirmed PC
- Stringent definition (some institutions):
  - ≥3 first-degree relatives with PC
- Family history found in ~5% to 10% of PC cases
- Having a family history confers a 9-fold greater risk than not having one

## Familial PC: Genetic Initiatives
- 2017 Australian Pancreatic Cancer Genome Initiative:
  - 10% to 20% of PCs likely have an inherited component
  - Deleterious mutations in BRCA1, BRCA2, MLH1, ATM, PALB2, CDK2NA
  - Mismatch repair gene mutations (Lynch syndrome)
- Germline mutations detected in 7% of patients unselected for family history
- Johns Hopkins National Familial Pancreas Tumor Registry:
  - 2-fold increased risk in 1st-degree relatives of sporadic PC
  - 9-fold increased risk in 1st-degree relatives of familial PC

## Familial PC: Specific Mutations & Blood Types
- BRCA2 germline mutations:
  - Found in 6% to 19% of familial PC patients
- Stringent definition (≥3 affected family members):
  - 57-fold increased risk
  - Incidence rate: 301 cases per 100,000/year (vs US average 8.8)
- PALB2 gene:
  - Germline truncating mutation in 3% of familial PC patients
- ABO Blood Groups:
  - Increased risk in A, B, and AB blood types
  - Attributed to ABO single nucleotide polymorphism, rs505922
  - Non-O blood group accounts for 13% to 19% of PDAC

## Table 61.3: High-Risk Genetic Syndromes (Part 1)
- Hereditary pancreatitis (PRSS1): 50-80x risk
- Lynch Syndrome (hMSH2, etc.): Undefined risk
- Hereditary breast/ovarian cancer (BRCA2): 3.5-10x risk
- FAMMM syndrome (p16): 20-34x risk
- Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11): 75-132x risk
- Ataxia-telangiectasia (ATM): Undefined risk

## Table 61.3: High-Risk Genetic Syndromes (Part 2)
- Collectively account for <5% of familial aggregation
- Mean age of onset similar to nonfamilial cases (~65 years)
- Familial cases have increased incidence of secondary primary cancers (23.8%) vs nonfamilial (18.9%)
- No single "pancreatic cancer gene" has been identified

## Hereditary Pancreatitis (HP)
- Autosomal dominant inherited disease
- Begins in childhood or adolescence with severe pancreatitis
- Results from germline/new somatic mutations in PRSS1 cationic trypsinogen gene (7q35)
- Lifetime risk of PC: 50% to 80% (50- to 80-fold increased risk)
- Risk seems limited to the pancreas (not other organs)

## HP: Interaction with Smoking
- Cigarette smoking is a major compounding factor
- ~40% of those with HP will develop PC if they also smoke
- Smoking in combination with HP may lower the age at diagnosis
- Highlights the multiplicative interaction between genetic mutations and environmental factors

## Hereditary Nonpolyposis Colorectal Cancer (Lynch Syndrome)
- Autosomal dominant inherited disease
- Predisposes to colorectal cancer and PC
- Caused by germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes:
  - MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2
- Estimated to develop PC at 8x the rate of the general population
- Least strongly linked to PC among inherited syndromes

## Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer (HBOC)
- BRCA2 mutations:
  - Up to 10-fold increased risk (range 3.5-10x) of PC
  - Even without strong family history of breast cancer
  - Found in 7% of sporadic PC patients screened
- BRCA1 mutations:
  - 3-fold increased risk of PC
  - 2-fold increased risk for colon cancer
  - 4-fold increased risk for gastric cancer
  - 120-fold increased risk for fallopian tube cancer

## Familial Atypical Multiple Mole Melanoma (FAMMM)
- Rare condition
- Associated with p16 germline mutations (9p21)
- p16 is a tumor suppressor gene (mutated or altered by methylation)
- Predisposes to:
  - Melanomas
  - Multiple nevi, atypical nevi
  - PC
- 20- to 34-fold increased risk of PC over lifetime

## Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome
- Rare autosomal dominant disease
- Associated with alterations in STK11 gene (19p13)
- Clinical features:
  - Hamartomatous polyps of GI tract
  - Lip freckles (mucocutaneous melanocytic macules)
- ~100-fold (75-132x) increased risk of developing PC
- Tendency to form intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs)

## Ataxia-Telangiectasia
- Autosomal recessive inherited disorder
- Associated with ATM gene mutations (11q22-23)
- Clinical features:
  - Cerebellar ataxia
  - Conjunctival telangiectasias
  - Hypofunctioning thymus gland
  - Oculomotor abnormalities
- Association with PC development is reported but less well established than other syndromes

## Cigarette Smoking: Causative Agent
- Definitively identified as causative agent in 25% to 35% of PDAC cases
- Most consistently reported risk factor
- Associated with increased risk in ≥29 epidemiologic studies
- Smokers have a 70% increased risk compared with nonsmokers
- IARC confirms smoking is casually related to PDAC

## Cigarette Smoking: Mortality Impact
- Contributes to death in PDAC patients
- Meta-analysis of 20 studies (2,517,623 patients, 15,341 deaths):
  - Current smokers: Hazard Ratio for death = 1.56 (CI 1.34-1.83)
  - Former smokers: Hazard Ratio = 1.15 (CI 1.06-1.26)
- Effect is independent of alcohol use, BMI, and diabetes

## Cigarette Smoking: US Prevalence
- ~15% or 40 million Americans continue to smoke
- Varies by race/ethnicity:
  - White men: 15.1% | White women: 13%
  - African American men: 21% | African American women: 13%
  - Hispanic men: 15% | Hispanic women: 8%
  - Asian men: 12.6% | Asian women: 3.5%
- Highest rates: American Indian/Alaskan Native
- Higher prevalence in rural areas and southern states

## Cigarette Smoking: Duration and Quitting
- Smoking habits in 13 years preceding diagnosis are most relevant
- Former smokers who quit for >13 years:
  - Risk decreases to that of lifetime nonsmokers
- Meta-analysis of 83 studies:
  - Overall relative risk in current/former smokers = 1.74 (74% increased risk)
- Retrospective analysis:
  - 57% (familial) and 60% (sporadic) reported prolonged smoking
  - Mean: 35 packs/year history

## Cigarette Smoking: Dose-Response
- Dose-response relationship documented between PDAC and number of cigarettes consumed
- Current smokers with family history of PC:
  - Relative risk as high as 8.23
- Individuals with familial PC tend to smoke more than sporadic cases
- Younger age at diagnosis in familial PC vs sporadic
- Suggests smoking interacts multiplicatively with genetic mutations

## Cigarette Smoking: Pathology
- Postmortem examinations of smokers' pancreatic ducts:
  - Widespread ductal hyperplasia
  - Lesions termed pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN)
  - Considered premalignant lesions
- Relationship with second malignancies:
  - PC as second malignancy in patients with smoking-related first malignancy (lung, head/neck, bladder)
  - Due to overlapping smoking-related genetic mutations

## Cigarette Smoking: Mechanisms
- Carcinogens cleared from bloodstream, excreted into bile, reach pancreas via biliary-pancreatic reflux or direct bloodstream carry
- Smoke contains >60 known carcinogens (PAHs, nitrosamines, benzo[a]pyrene, etc.)
- Mechanisms:
  - Bind to DNA, form adducts, increase somatic mutations
  - Nitrosamines are organ-specific (cause pancreatic carcinomas in hamsters)
  - Higher cholesterol levels (nicotinic stimulation of catecholamines)
  - Chronic inflammation induction
  - Integral to reactivation of metastatic disease

## Environmental Tobacco Smoke (ETS)
- Related to PC development with likely dose-response relationship
- Mildly elevated odds ratio (OR 1.21) in nonsmokers exposed as adult and child
- Effect more pronounced in smokers with ETS exposure
- Nonsmokers exposed to ETS early in life (<21 years):
  - Diagnosed at significantly younger mean age (64.0 vs 66.5 years)
- Both smoking and ETS in youth associated with younger diagnosis in familial, sporadic, and Ashkenazi Jewish cases

## ETS: Surgeon General Report
- 2006 US Surgeon General determination:
  - Second-hand smoke contains ≥69 human carcinogens
  - No safe exposure level
- >45,000 annual deaths in US from lung cancer and heart disease
- Occurs in persons with no personal smoking history but exposed to secondhand smoke

## Cigars and Waterpipe Smoking
- Cigars:
  - Contain same carcinogens as cigarettes
  - Increased risk for lung, oropharyngeal, larynx, esophageal cancers
  - 4 to 10x risk of dying from these cancers
- Waterpipe smoking:
  - Reported by 4% of high school students regularly
  - Considered more socially acceptable
  - Smoke moves through water filter, implying less harm
  - Delivers same toxins; adverse effects under investigation

## E-Cigarettes
- Aerosolized delivery system of nicotine (emerged early 2000s)
- Liquid contains: nicotine, propylene glycol, vegetable glycerin, flavorings
- Usage trends (2017-2018):
  - Increased 78% among high school students
  - 3% of adults report current use
- >200 possible cases of severe pulmonary disease reported
- Long-term association with PC remains to be determined

## Smokeless Tobacco
- Includes dry snuff, chewing tobacco, snus, dissolvable nicotine products
- Sales increasing faster than cigarettes
- Promoted as safer alternative and smoking cessation method
- Reality:
  - No evidence it is effective for smoking cessation
  - Causes oral cancer, esophageal cancer, and PC
  - Causes bone loss around teeth and nicotine addiction

## High-Risk Occupations: Challenges
- Evidence linking occupational exposures to PC is inconsistent
- Difficulties in quantification:
  - Workplace exposure to carcinogens
  - Differentiating from other risk factors
  - Self-reported exposures
  - Lack of objective quantitative monitoring data
  - Personal comorbidities and confounding factors
- Overall occupational etiologic fraction estimated at 12% (meta-analysis of 20 studies, 1969-1998)

- Chemical processor: OR 1.22
- Chemical fertilizer: OR 1.20
- Chemist: MH 10.2
- Auto mechanic (gasoline): RR 5.1 (if >10 yrs exposure)
- Service station worker: SMR 1.6
- Machine repairer: OR 2.45
- Dry cleaner: RR 2.1
- Leather tanner: MH 3.1
- Oil refinery worker: OR 2.11
- Aluminum mill worker: SMR 125.2

- Floor polisher: SMR 1.3
- Electrical assembler/installer: OR 2.20
- Metalworker: SMR 2.0
- Manufacturing plant worker: SMR 3.0
- Assembly worker: SMR 3.0
- Foundry and engine plant workers: SMR 3.0
- Plant/system operator: OR 6.1
- Pharmacist, dietician, therapist: OR 7.1

- Methylene chloride (chlorinated hydrocarbons):
  - Spray paints: OR 1.61
  - Paint strippers: OR 1.40
  - Aerosol propellant: RR 1.6
- Pesticides/herbicides:
  - Corn wet milling: OR 1.4
  - DDT (Farming): RR 4.8
  - DDD (Flight attendants): RR 4.3
  - Ethylan: RR 5.0

- Cotton dust (Farming): OR 4.37
- Cement (Construction): OR 1.28
- Lead (Various): OR 1.28
- Metalworking fluids (Machinist): OR 2.0
- Retrospective analysis of 22 studies:
  - Most common: asbestos, pesticides, residential radon, coal products, welding, radiation

## Metalworking Fluids (MWFs)
- NIOSH review of 5 cohort studies:
  - Association between MWFs (industrial machining/grinding) and all types of cancer, including PDAC
- >1 million workers exposed to MWFs
- Increased risk at several sites: pancreas, larynx, rectum, skin, scrotum, bladder
- MWFs contain suspected initiators/promoters:
  - Long-chain aliphatics, PAHs, nitrosamines
  - Sulfur-containing compounds, formaldehyde-releasing biocides, heavy metals

## Diabetes: Bidirectional Relationship
- Diabetes and prediabetes are risk factors AND consequences of PC
- 50% to 80% of PDAC patients have subclinical impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes at diagnosis
- PC causes alteration of islet cell function:
  - Loss of b-cell mass from tumor growth
  - Disruptions in acinar-islet cell interactions

## Diabetes: Mechanisms
- Chronic hyperinsulinemia and hyperglycemia proposed as underlying mechanisms
- Experimental evidence:
  - Insulin promotes proliferation and reduces apoptosis in PC cells
  - Directly and indirectly via increased IGF bioavailability
- Hyperglycemia enhances proliferation and invasion capability
- Meta-analysis: every 0.56 mmol/L increase in fasting blood glucose = 14% increase in PC rate

## Diabetes: Long-term and New-Onset
- Population-based case-control study:
  - Diabetes diagnosed ≥10 years before PDAC: 50% increased risk
  - Insulin treatment did not alter risk (OR 1.6 with vs 1.5 without)
- New-onset diabetes:
  - Self-reported history of new-onset diabetes before PC diagnosis in 26% and 31% of study populations

## Diabetes: Diet and BMI Interactions
- Nurses’ Health Study (18-year follow-up):
  - Positive association between fructose intake, impaired glucose metabolism, and PC risk
  - Risk most apparent in women with BMI >30 kg/m2 and low physical activity
- High glycemic load diet increases risk in women with underlying insulin resistance
- Chronically elevated plasma glucose levels further support impaired glucose tolerance/insulin resistance in PC etiology

## Pancreatitis: Population Attributable Risk
- Widely studied risk factor
- Population-attributable fraction: 1.34% (34% excess risk) in analysis of 10 pooled studies
- Association stronger when pancreatitis occurred >3 years before PC diagnosis (OR 4.0)
- Cellular destruction and glandular dysfunction may yield environment favoring tumor initiation

## Acute Pancreatitis (AP)
- May be the initial clinical presentation of PDAC
- Precedes malignant diagnosis by weeks or months
- Veterans Health Administration retrospective study:
  - 10.7% of veterans diagnosed with PC had history of AP within 2 years
  - Risk greatest in first year after AP episode
  - Further elevated in persons ≥70 years of age

## Chronic Pancreatitis (CP)
- Linked to PC development
- Standardized incidence ratio of PDAC in CP patients: 16.5 (vs 1.76 expected)
- Swedish inpatient review (1965-1983):
  - 7956 patients with pancreatitis
  - 46 PCs diagnosed vs 21 expected (SIR 2.2)
- Pooled results from 7 studies:
  - 13-fold higher risk of PC in CP patients (RR 13.3)

## CP vs. IPMN Diagnostic Challenges
- Problematic conclusion regarding CP as a pure risk factor:
  - Some premalignant lesions like IPMNs may be initially incorrectly diagnosed as CP
  - Clouds arguments concerning chronic pancreatitis as an independent risk factor
  - Highlights the need for accurate histological diagnosis in longitudinal studies

## Pancreatic Cysts
- Fairly common, often incidentally found on MRI/CT
- Present in general population at rates of 2.6% to 15% or higher
- Some represent premalignant lesions (IPMN, MCN)
- 75% of PDACs arise from solid lesions, ~25% from cystic lesions
- Risk increases with cyst size:
  - Beyond 3 cm, risk of cancer estimated at 18% to 25%
- Removing premalignant cysts at appropriate time reduces PDAC incidence

## Lifestyle: Height and Weight (BMI)
- HPFS and NHS large prospective cohort studies
- Higher risk among obese men and women:
  - 10% higher for overweight
  - 20% higher in obese vs normal-weight
- 5-unit increase in BMI = 10% excess risk of PC
- Proportion of PC attributable to obesity: 3% to 16%
- Direct association between above-average height and PC risk:
  - Additional 2.54 cm height = 6% (HPFS) to 10% (NHS) increased risk

## Lifestyle: Height as a Proxy
- Association between height and general cancer risk identified in other studies
- Pooled meta-analytical study found no association between height and PC
- Height may serve as a proxy for:
  - Calorie intake
  - Exposure to growth factors (insulin, IGF-1) in childhood

## Lifestyle: Physical Inactivity
- Proportion of all cancers attributable to physical inactivity: ~3%
- Inverse relationship between moderate physical activity and PC
- Walking/hiking ≥1.5 hours/week in overweight cohort:
  - 50% reduction in PC risk
- BMI had no effect on risk if participant was moderate exerciser
- BMI ≥30 kg/m2 had elevated risk (RR 1.72) vs BMI <23 kg/m2

## Diet: Fats and Cholecystokinin
- 30% to 50% of PCs may be attributable to dietary factors
- Butter consumption and saturated fat intake positively associated with PDAC risk
- Higher consumption of saturated fat/calorie-rich foods influences mortality trends
- Mechanism hypothesis:
  - Fat entering duodenum stimulates cholecystokinin secretion
  - Chronic hypercholecystokininemia may increase susceptibility to carcinogens
- Alternative: Saturated fat leads to insulin resistance/diabetes, or foods contaminated with organochlorides

## Diet: Processed Meats
- Processed meats linked to PC development
- Prospective study (>200,000 people, 7 years):
  - Greatest consumption of processed meats = 67% increased risk
- Diets laden with pork and red meat = 50% increase in risk
- Poultry, fish, dairy, eggs conferred no additional risk
- Carcinogens: Heterocyclic amines and PAHs formed during high-temperature cooking (barbecued meats)

## Diet: Glycemic Load and Sugars
- Conflicting results on fruit juices, soda, glycemic load, and sugar intake
- Two studies found no relationship
- Three studies reported mixed findings
- Multiethnic Cohort Study:
  - BMI modified effect of high sucrose intake
  - Elevated BMI increased risk, normal BMI decreased risk
- Positive association with high fructose intake, but no association with soft drinks

## Coffee and Alcohol: Historical Confounding
- 1970s/1980s cohort studies indicated heavy coffee/alcohol led to excess PDAC risk
- Often confounded by excessive smoking among heavy drinkers
- 2002 Swedish study hypothesis:
  - Examined alcoholics with CP or cirrhosis
  - 40% excess risk observed
  - Authors estimated excess risk "may be almost totally attributable to confounding effect of smoking"

## Coffee and Alcohol: NHS & HPFS Findings
- Large national cohort studies (1,907,222 person-years, 288 incident cases)
- Results revealed NO excess risk for coffee or alcohol:
  - >3 cups coffee/day vs none: Pooled RR 0.62
  - >30g alcohol/day vs none: Pooled RR 1.00
- Turati et al. (2011) meta-analysis (37 case-control, 17 cohort):
  - Adjusted for smoking
  - Concluded coffee consumption not appreciably related to PC, even at high doses

## Alcohol: Heavy Consumption Meta-Analyses
- Two recent meta-analyses found heavy alcohol increases PC risk
- Pooled meta-analysis (19 studies, 4,211,129 persons):
  - Light/moderate: little to no influence
  - Heavy (>24g/day): RR 1.15 to 1.43 increase
- PanC4 Consortium:
  - Light to moderate (~4 drinks/day): no association
  - High consumption (9 drinks/day): OR 1.6
  - Persisted after adjusting for smoking and excluding pancreatitis history

## Infectious Agents: H. pylori and HBV
- Helicobacter pylori:
  - Moderate risk factor (analysis of 7 studies)
  - Global prevalence 25-50% in Westernized countries
  - Estimated 25-45% of PC cases in these countries may involve H. pylori
- Hepatitis B virus (HBV):
  - Chronic infection increases PDAC risk (OR 1.42) in blood group A individuals
  - HBV can infect pancreas and liver
  - 40% to 60% excess risk of PC in HBV-positive persons

## Infectious Agents: Microbiome
- 2017 systematic review of gut microbiome:
  - Lower levels of Neisseria elongate and Streptococcus mitis
  - High levels of Porphyromonas gingivalis and Granulicatella adiacens
  - Associated with increased risk of PC
- Highlights emerging role of oral and gut microbiota in pancreatic carcinogenesis

## Summary: Modifiable Risk Factors
- PDAC etiology is multifactorial
- Certain risk factors are amenable to modification
- Nearly two-thirds of major, noninherited genetic risk factors are modifiable
- Opportunities for prevention through:
  - Increased public awareness
  - Screening high-risk individuals
  - Promotion of healthier lifestyles

## Summary Strategy 1: Tobacco Cessation
- Avoid use and proximity to tobacco products
- Do not start smoking; quit if currently smoking cigarettes or cigars
- Do not use smokeless tobacco products
- Avoid persons actively smoking; ask smokers not to smoke in the home
- Discourage cigars, waterpipe, e-cigarettes, smokeless tobacco
- Refer smokers to smoking cessation programs

## Summary Strategy 2: Diet and Exercise
- Make healthy dietary and exercise modifications
- Reduce weight through menu-based and calorie restriction programs if overweight/obese
- Consider surgical obesity intervention if appropriate
- Increase daily intake of fruits and vegetables
- Reduce simple carbohydrates and saturated fats
- Avoid processed meats, limit red meat, increase fish/poultry
- Increase physical activity (20 mins moderate exercise, 3-5x/week)

## Summary Strategy 3: Occupational Protections
- Consider occupational and environmental exposures
- For individuals in high-risk occupations or environmental exposure:
  - Regular use of OSHA-recommended personal protective equipment (PPE)
  - Will minimize risk of carcinogen exposure

## Summary Strategy 4: Screening High-Risk Individuals
- Screen to detect precursor lesions and early-stage tumors
- High-risk individuals include:
  - Older smokers with new-onset diabetes
  - Persons experiencing unintentional weight loss
  - Individuals with suspicious pancreatic/biliary lesions found incidentally
  - People with family history of pancreatic or related cancers

## Conclusion
- Considerable epidemiologic data points to largely avoidable PC causes
- Multilayered therapeutic resistance remains a challenge for advanced PDAC
- Early detection and prevention strategies are critical
- Bending the curve on the predicted rise of PC requires comprehensive public health and clinical interventions
- Continued research into genetic and environmental interactions is essential

## Key Takeaways
- PDAC is the 4th leading cause of cancer death, predicted to be 2nd by 2030
- Smoking, obesity, diabetes, and chronic pancreatitis are major modifiable risk factors
- Familial and genetic syndromes account for a small but significant high-risk group
- Occupational exposures and diet play contributory roles
- Lifestyle modifications and targeted screening offer the best hope for reducing global burden

## Global Burden Summary
- PC ranks 12th among all cancers globally but 7th in cancer-related deaths
- Disparities exist globally, with highest rates in Eastern Europe and South America
- Lowest rates observed in parts of Africa and Asia
- Understanding global distribution aids in targeting public health interventions
- Continued surveillance is necessary as incidence rates continue to rise in many regions
